title: The Threshold Theorem
summary: Concatenated codes push the logical error rate down doubly exponentially when the physical rate is below a threshold.
objectives: Compute the logical error rate after several levels of concatenation of the three-qubit code
Find the pseudo-threshold as a fixed point of the error map, and say what happens on each side of it
Work out how many levels and physical qubits a target error rate needs
Say what fault tolerance adds to a code, and how the threshold of the theorem differs from the pseudo-threshold
mission: Each level of a code feeds its own output to the next, and this exercise follows that for the three-qubit bit-flip code. One level, with perfect correction, maps a physical error probability p to f(p) = 3p² − 2p³. Write f(p), and concatenated(p, k), the error rate after k levels (f applied k times). Write generic_rate(p, c, k) = (c·p)^(2^k) / c. Write levels_needed(p, target), the smallest k with concatenated(p, k) ≤ target, or None if the error rate never gets that low. Set p_th to the pseudo-threshold of f, the fixed point with 0 < p < 1. For p = 0.01 and target = 1e-15, store the number of levels in k_needed and the number of physical qubits per logical qubit (3 per level, so 3^k) in qubits.

prediction.question: From p = 0.02, one level of the three-qubit code gives f(p) = 0.001184. What error rate does the second level give?
prediction.explanation: The second level applies the same map to the first level's output: f(0.001184) = 3 × 0.001184² − 2 × 0.001184³ ≈ 4.2 × 10⁻⁶. Squaring alone forgets the factor 3, the three pairs of qubits that can fail. Each level squares the error rate, so the improvement grows from level to level instead of repeating a fixed factor.

hints: concatenated(p, k) applies f to p, k times. What does the loop have to do with p at each step? For generic_rate, the formula is in the mission.

The pseudo-threshold is the fixed point 0 < p < 1 of f: solve 3p² − 2p³ = p, which reduces to 2p² − 3p + 1 = 0. In levels_needed, if p is not below p_th the rate never decreases, so there is no level to return.

Below p_th, start at k = 0 and apply f until the value is at most target, counting the steps. k_needed = levels_needed(0.01, 1e-15), and each level replaces every qubit by three, so you need 3**k physical qubits. Printing concatenated(0.01, k) for k = 0, 1, 2, ... is a good check.

challenge.mission: A larger code corrects more errors, and it also offers more pairs of locations where two errors can meet. Take a distance-3 code on 7 qubits in a counting model that is a simplification: a block fails whenever 2 or more of its 7 qubits have an error, so every pair of errors is fatal, and the kind of error and the correction circuit are ignored. One level then maps p to f7(p) = 1 − (1−p)⁷ − 7p(1−p)⁶, about 21p² for small p. Write f7(p); fixed_point(step, lo, hi), which finds by bisection the p in [lo, hi] with step(p) = p, given that step(lo) < lo and step(hi) > hi; and levels_for(step, p, target), the number of levels that bring p to target or below, or None when a level does not lower the error rate. Store in p7_th the nonzero fixed point of f7 (it lies between 0.01 and 0.5), in k7 the levels f7 needs to take p = 10⁻³ to 10⁻¹⁵ or below, in qubits7 the physical qubits that takes (each level replaces every qubit by seven, so 7^k7), and in k3 the levels the mission's f needs for the same task. The validator calls your three functions on maps and inputs of its own, including a map you have not seen.
hints: The mission's levels_needed fixes both f and the threshold. Which two things must become arguments so that one function can serve f, f7 and a map the validator invents?

Bisection on step(p) − p: it is negative at lo and positive at hi, so keep the half of the interval where the sign changes. In levels_for, apply step until p is at most target, and return None as soon as step(p) is not smaller than p, since the rate has stopped falling.

p7_th = fixed_point(f7, 0.01, 0.5), k7 = levels_for(f7, 1e-3, 1e-15) and k3 = levels_for(f, 1e-3, 1e-15). Print p7_th and compare it with 1/21: 1/21 is lower than the true value, because 21p² overestimates f7 once p is not small.
